opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the areas where academics actually have a comparative advantage, and that's rare right now. If you're in a university lab, you're never going to out-scale the frontier labs on pretraining. You don't have the compute, you don't have the data pipelines, you don't have the infrastructure teams. So if you try to compete on "who can train the biggest, best model," you're going to lose, and a lot of that work ends up being incremental or quickly made obsolete.

Interpretability is different. A lot of the most important progress has come from fairly small models, careful thinking, and good taste in experiment design. You can learn an enormous amount from a model that fits on a single GPU. The open-weight models that are available now are more than capable enough to study real phenomena, like how features are represented, how circuits compose, and what's actually going on when a model does in-context learning or multi-step reasoning. The bottleneck there isn't compute. It's ideas and rigor, which is exactly what academia is supposed to be good at.

It also matters a lot. We're building systems that are getting more capable very quickly, and our ability to understand what's happening inside them is lagging well behind. If we could reliably look inside a model and say "here's why it gave that answer," or "here's the representation it's using for deception, or for its goals," that changes the picture for safety, and it changes how much we can trust these systems in high-stakes settings. It's one of those problems where real progress has a very high payoff.

And there's a lot of low-hanging fruit. The field is still young enough that a smart grad student can pick a well-defined question, like "how does this model represent X?", dig into it properly, and produce something genuinely new that the labs will read and build on. That's a much better position than writing the hundredth paper on a slightly tweaked fine-tuning method that'll be irrelevant in six months.

So it's a combination of three things: it fits academic resources, it's intellectually deep, and it's important. I'd love to see a lot more of the talent in universities pointed at it.

r004.rationale: It favors interpretability and understanding model behavior over another incremental fine-tuning paper, which it describes as quickly becoming irrelevant.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that interpretability is one of the few places where the comparative advantage of academia is really clear right now, and it's a bit frustrating to watch so much of the field chase problems where it just can't compete.

If you think about what a lot of academic ML research looks like today, it's trying to push the frontier on capabilities with a fraction of the compute that the labs have. You're training a small model, you show some trick works at that scale, and then the open question is always: does this hold at a hundred or a thousand times the compute? Often it doesn't, and the labs have already run that experiment internally and know the answer. So you end up doing work that's either already been done or that won't transfer. That's a demoralizing position to be in.

Interpretability is almost the opposite. The frontier of understanding is really, really far behind the frontier of capability. We have these systems that can do remarkable things, and we have only the faintest idea of what's actually going on inside them. The gap is enormous, and crucially, a lot of the important questions don't require a frontier model to study. You can learn deep things about how transformers represent concepts, how circuits form, how features superpose, on models that fit on a single GPU or even a laptop. The open-weight models are good enough now that there's an incredible amount of territory to explore. So the compute barrier that cuts academia out of capabilities research mostly doesn't apply here.

It's also just a wonderful kind of science. It feels much more like early neuroscience or early biology than engineering. You're looking at an organism nobody designed in detail, and you're trying to figure out how it works. That rewards exactly the things universities are good at: careful methodology, long time horizons, people who are willing to go deep on a weird question for three years without needing it to ship.

And then there's the stakes. If these systems keep getting more capable, the question of whether we can actually verify what they're doing, as opposed to just observing their behavior, becomes one of the most important questions there is. Behavioral evals only tell you so much. Being able to look inside and say, this model is or isn't representing something, this is or isn't the mechanism driving the output, that's the kind of thing that could matter a lot. The labs are working on it, but there are just not that many people, and the problem is huge. I'd love for there to be a thousand grad students attacking it from angles nobody inside a lab would think to try.

So when I see a brilliant PhD student spending their time on a slightly better optimizer that may or may not matter at scale, part of me wants to say: there's this whole open field right here, you have everything you need to work on it, and the results would actually compound.

r001.rationale: The response says labs have already run large-scale experiments and know whether small-scale results transfer, leaving academics doing work that may be duplicative or fail at scale.

r002.rationale: It describes interpretability questions as open territory that researchers can explore with open-weight models, and says this work suits universities.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says important interpretability questions can be studied on models that fit on a single GPU or laptop.

r004.rationale: It urges academic researchers to pursue deep scientific understanding of models rather than incremental capability work such as slightly better optimizers.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention ChatGPT or connect its demonstration of deep learning’s usefulness to greater receptiveness toward interpretability.

astra-6.text:
Because I think it’s both incredibly important and an area where academia can make real progress. If you’re trying to push the frontier of model capabilities, you’re increasingly competing with organizations that can spend enormous amounts on compute and run hundreds of experiments. That’s a difficult position for an academic lab.

With interpretability, you can take an existing model and ask a question we don’t know how to answer: How is it actually doing this? What representations has it learned? Why does a particular intervention change its behavior? There’s room for a small group with a good idea to discover something fundamental.

And the gap between what we can build and what we understand is extraordinary. We can train these systems to do increasingly sophisticated things, but we can’t reliably look inside them and explain the computation that produced an answer. As we give them more responsibility, that seems like a very consequential gap to close.

I also think it’s a wonderful scientific problem. You have this complicated object that you can inspect, run experiments on, and modify. You can test causal explanations of its behavior. That seems like exactly the kind of work universities should be exceptionally good at.

r001.rationale: It says academic labs struggle to compete with frontier organizations’ compute and experiment volume, but does not say they lack feedback about what works at scale or that this makes choosing worthwhile problems harder.

r002.rationale: The response presents interpretability as an area where small groups can make progress, but does not state that its problems are legible to researchers outside major AI labs.

r003.rationale: It contrasts interpretability work using existing models and small groups with capability research requiring enormous compute and many experiments, conveying that interpretability does not need enormous computational resources.

r004.rationale: It argues for interpretability’s importance and scientific value, but does not advocate prioritizing understanding over incremental model improvements.

r005.rationale: ChatGPT is not mentioned, and the response offers no explanation involving its demonstration of deep learning’s usefulness.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think it’s one of the areas where academia could make a really big contribution without needing to compete directly with the labs on compute. You can study a model that already exists and ask, “What algorithm did it learn? How does it represent this concept? Why does changing this activation change its behavior?” Those are deep scientific questions, and answering them could be useful well beyond the particular model you’re studying.

The thing I’d love is for us to get better at understanding what’s actually going on inside these systems. We’re very good at measuring what a model can do, but much less good at explaining how it does it. And that gap matters if you want to know whether you can trust its behavior in a situation you haven’t tested.

That also seems like a natural fit for academic research: developing an understanding that other people can build on, rather than having to train the next frontier model yourself.
